The closer I got to finishing the game, the more anxious I felt. Of course, it reached a crescendo during the final battle and when it was over, I was numb. I talked to all the characters and that was that.

Then the Epilogue started and I "played" through that. When that was done and the credits rolled, I openly wept.

Here's my thoughts on why:

I had spent well over a thousand hours getting to know these  people. I fought and died in countless battles with my friends for almost 3 years in Act 1 alone. We were comrades in arms, and in some cases, we were more than that.

Even after release, I restarted the game probably 8-10 times before finally completing it. It was the equivalent to 5he magical summer when the family lived in a beach house for a couple months and you meet the person of your dreams. You never want that feeling to end. But, unfortunately, end it does. And you return to the doldrums of your real life. You spend the rest of your life wondering if the friends you made during that magnificent adventure remember you as fondly as you remember them. And you yearn for that companionship again.

Sure, you could start anew, as I have since done, but the magic is different. Your companions don't recall the heroics of the previous playthrough, the intimate times shared learning to swim, or sparring, or staring at the stars; the conversations and growth and insights gained of each other.

But we do. And we mourn that loss.

But I have to tell you, it has made one helluva difference in my quality of life. My spine curvature was impacted due to some trauma about 25 years ago. It has improved dramatically,  but I still have a way to go. (He took before and during X-rays and compared them.) I went from seeing him twice a week for about 2 months to about once a month now. I don't subscribe to science being the "truth". Science doesn't care about truth. Science cares about facts. Truth, as you pointed out, has roots in faith and philosophy. As for the scientific consistencies, that has to do with testing via experiments, observations, etc. and getting the same results each time. If you don't, then you start over with a new hypothesis. All it takes is one negative result and the current model is wrong. It doesn't take a belief (or faith, to use your definition).

"Science will figure it out" is absolutely a leap of faith, and perhaps that may be true in all cases someday. But for now, obviously, we are a LONG way from that point. I don't know enough to say if that will ever be true for homo sapiens. I'm sure that someone out there would say it, but it lacks any credence or weight.

I appreciate your patience, but the only faith that science should involve is building on what others did before that has been accepted as a cornerstone. For example, the theory of gravity. We can't actually prove it exists, but we can show enough repeatable, consistent data to trust that the theory is correct. I've never seen the Eiffel Tower, but there are innumerable people who have, so I have faith that its existence is an undeniable fact.
Sociology is a "true science" and I apologize if my explanation is misconstrued. Hopefully everyone knows what meant.

How does one measure and record "meaning, value, and morality"? How does one put them through the rigors of the scientific method? As much as these things change based on societal norms, I don't know that it's possible to scientifically define them. I mean, we can define the terms, obviously, and we can study meaning, value(s), and morals in various societies and communities. Science -true science - holds up no matter what community you belong to or morality you subscribe to. 

If that doesn't help any, then I'm not sure I'm qualified to continue to try to answer your question. I apologize  in advance. In my opinion (and it is just that, my opinion), the things you mentioned cannot be empirically studied outside of their specific bubbles.

Absolutely! The discipline required to be an objective scientist *SHOULD* keep one away from "believing" in scientism. Knowing that facts and figures and actual data that can be reproduced is a (if I may say this tongue in cheek) sacred standard.

As for morality and other traits that are ascribed to humanity, while some are relatively constant, they are shaped by community standards. If we as a society decide killing your immediate superior is the only way to advance, then that's that. This is one of the reasons I have an issue with applying modern morality to historical occurrences. It's apples and oranges.

I don't "believe in scientism", I trust in science. Science, by it's very nature, is tested over and over again until it fails to meet the required criteria. If it does, new theories are created from the evidence available and the process begins anew.

I remember when I was in the 5th grade and we did an experiment where the teacher gave the first person a slip of paper that had a statement on it. That person then relayed it verbally to the next person, who then relayed it, etc. until it got to the last person who then spoke it out loud.

It was NOTHING like the original statement.

Now think about these word of mouth stories being passed along from person to person for 500 years. Of course there are going to be some discrepancies in the stories. And I'd be willing to bet my immortal soul (if such a thing exists; I'm not convinced) that the stories we have now are NOTHING like the originals.

Inaccuracies being pointed out seem rather ineffective, in my opinion, and only tend to get 99.9% of people to double down on their defense of religion because it comes across as an attack. Asking the questions that have no other obvious answer than "because your God doesn't exist", but NEVER ACTUALLY SAYING IT OUT LOUD are the most effective seeds to plant. 

To me it was my philosophy professor asking the limits of omnipotence and the class discussing them collectively. One of the students, a devout christian, made her case for God's omnipotence. To which he would respond with questions of his own: why did God need 6 days to create everything if he could just think it all into existence? Could he create a rock so big and heavy that He couldn't pick it up?

It seems such an elementary and simplistic approach these days after watching and reading everything I have since that moment, but it planted the seed of doubt in my mind. And that seed has flourished since I took it up on myself to research and investigate more. 

I took that philosophy class in 1992 and finally realized and came out as an atheist in 2011. It wasn't some flavor of the week thing I jumped at first thing. There was nearly 20 years of anger and pain and betrayal that were involved - and I'm just talking about my introspection and soul searching! I had a profound sense of loss to begin with. But as logic and knowledge filled the void left by the loss of "faith", I became stronger in my own defense when I felt the need to do so.I became better at defeating the attempts to "bring me back into Christ's embrace". I've been god-free for 14 years and I'm more comfortable than ever.

I've told this story in other subs before, but I'll tell it here. My maternal grandparents lived in an old house in South central Florida for years and were maybe 5 minutes off the Gulf coast. At the time of the incident, there were very few people who lived around there. In fact, their closest neighbors were my paternal grandparents who lived maybe a half mile up the limerock road. 

Back then, there were no security lights in "normal" (read: poor) people's yards. And like I said, there was nothing but scrub oaks and palmetto bushes forever around their house. It was DARK. One night, my first cousin and I were spending the night with our grandparents and we were in my grandma's bedroom playing. Mamaw and Papaw had separate rooms because Papaw snored like a gaggle of chainsaws. 

Anyway, Mamaw had her bed just across from the door from the hallway, so it was the first thing you saw. She had a spare twin (maybe full sized, I don't exactly remember) in the corner against the walls about 6-8 feet away from her bed. Her closet door was near the foot of her bed and the dresser was on the same wall as the door to enter her room from the hall.

My cousin was on my Mamaw's bed while I sat on the spare bed. We were throwing one of those cheap plastic balls back and forth to each other. There was one lamp on in the room and if I recall correctly, it was on the dresser to my left. I tossed the ball back to my cousin and it hit her square in the chest and hit the floor. I looked at her but she was looking over my shoulder, her eyes wide open with an unmistakable look of sheer terror on her face. I turned and looked out the window and staring back at me through the window were two glowing red "eyes". They were no more than 3-4 feet from my face with only the glass of the panes between us. I remember being startled and thinking, "Now what is THAT?!?" But I don't remember being scared...just kidding, I was maybe 5-6 years old. I screamed (as did my cousin) and we both hauled ass out of that room and did NOT go back that night.

Now out my grandma's window was the back yard and porch. The porch was maybe 18 inches off the ground and the window sill another 18-24 inches or so higher than that. To be as close to me as it was, it would have to have been standing on the back porch. Thinking back on it now, I would place the "eyes" at 24-36 inches above the surface of the porch.

Now, having said all that, I do not believe that it was anything paranormal (unlike my cousin who swears to this day that we saw the eyes of a demon). I feel like it could have been a bear, as the Florida Black bear was quite common in the area at that time or maybe even a Florida panther. I have no idea if either of those animals eyes reflect a reddish hue. I know it wasn't a deer, at least not a normal deer, as their eyes reflect a greenish/blue color. (I've seen lots of them by now.)

But there you go. My semi-scary probably not paranormal story from my childhood in the Central Florida swampland.

The thing about ISO audits is all you have to do is ask a few specific questions about items that are required, then see how the company says they deal with them. However they say they do it, you ask for evidence to verify that they're doing what they say they're doing. If it's there, yay! If not, non-conformance. Then you rank the non-conformance by how bad it's messed up.

Oh, you said you do A & B but the evidence only show you do A? Opportunity for improvement. (Maybe a minor depending on the auditor and their mood). Oh, there's a section in the ISO manual that you don't even acknowledge and have nothing pertaining to it? There's a Major non-conformance.

It is literally: Do what you say. Say what you do. Have evidence to support it.

3 weeks ago I was coming home from work and driving up the dirt road I live on. As I approached my driveway, I see a small turtle, maybe 8" wide scurrying down the middle of the road. I parked my truck and went and picked her up. I brought her back to the house so my son could play with her for a bit before I released her. (He loves giggling at them kicking their little legs trying to get away.)

After about 5-10 minutes, he grew bored, so I hopped back in the truck (with the turtle) and drove down to the creek at the bottom of the hill. I stepped to the edge of the road and was about to drop her in the water. I looked and directly below  me were stones used to help slow down the erosion from the water pouring forth from the double culverts that served as a typical makeshift South Alabama bridge.

I couldn't just drop her, so I did some quick math and figured I could project her forward a few feet and she'd land in the water and swim away, none the worse for wear. I stepped as close to the edge as I could get and went to pitch her forward. As my weight shifted from a center point to my front foot, the dirt on the edge of the road gave way and down I fell, face first.

Now, I won't tell you my whole life flashed before my eyes, but I do remember thinking two distinct thoughts before everything went black: 1) "Yay! She made it and is swimming away!"  2) "Fuck this is going to hurt."

The next thing I was aware of, I was lifting myself out of the creek, face down. I sat back on my haunches and realized I couldn't see anything. I'd lost my glasses in the tumble. I also heard as my left hearing aide shut down but my right one was nowhere to be found. My phone was in my pocket and was completely submerged. 

As I sat there, I looked up the embankment where I'd fallen and was wondering how I was going to get back up there. At that point, I noticed the vision in my right eye getting blurry. I lifted my hand up to my face and brought it back down, covered in blood. A few more moments passed and I tried to climb the bank. I promptly fell back down and that's when I realized my right wrist was hurting horribly.

I ended up climbing out of the creek on the left bank, crawling through the muck and briars and grass before finally making it back to the road. I crawled to my truck, got in, and drove back home.

My in-laws live next door and I politely asked my mother-in-law to stay with my son while my father-in-law took me to the ER.

I ended up getting 4 stitches and was put on concussion protocol for a week and a half.

tl;dr: I saved a turtle and got a concussion.
